resolved_by: Supreme Court, United States v. Taylor, 596 U.S. 845 (2022), which affirmed the Fourth Circuit's Taylor decision and rejected the Government's position that an attempt to commit a completed crime of violence is itself a crime of violence.
issue: Is an attempt to commit a crime of violence, such as attempted Hobbs Act robbery, itself a crime of violence under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)?

sides.position: An attempt to commit a crime of violence is invariably a crime of violence, because § 924(c) reaches attempted use of force.
cases: United States v. Walker, 990 F.3d 316 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Smith, 957 F.3d 590 (5th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Ingram, 947 F.3d 1021 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Dominguez, 954 F.3d 1251 (9th Cir. 2020)
United States v. St. Hubert, 909 F.3d 335 (11th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: An attempt is a crime of violence only if the attempt itself involves actual, attempted, or threatened force; an attempt to threaten force is not an attempt to use force.
cases: United States v. Taylor, 979 F.3d 203 (4th Cir. 2020), aff'd, 596 U.S. 845 (2022)
United States v. Palmer, No. 21-4355 (4th Cir. 2024)

this_court: follows Taylor, the Fourth Circuit position as affirmed by the Supreme Court
quote: Our decision in Taylor created a split with our sister circuits, and the Supreme Court promptly took up the case.
cite: United States v. Raymond Palmer, No. 21-4355 (4th Cir. 2024)
